title: Using AI Well: A Blueprint for Teachers
author: Matthews, Paul
summary: Paul Matthews opens with a portrait of a flourishing teacher -- one with deep rest, meaningful work, continual improvement, equipped students, and creative exercise of craft -- and positions AI as something that can support those goals but also undermine them if adopted carelessly. Part 1 of his 8-step blueprint covers four practices: setting ethical Boundaries about what you will and won't use AI for (the process of deciding matters more than the exact lines); having a Vision for what you will do with the time AI saves (without a vision, the gravitational pull is simply to do more); Immersion in one tool mastered deeply rather than flitting between dozens; and Direction -- the art of prompting -- framed as an extension of the teacher's existing skill of explaining tasks clearly. The Role-Task-Format prompting structure he provides is deliberately simple: it maps onto what teachers already do every time they explain an assignment to students. The article is drawn from his book Wise AI and is addressed to teachers who want to flourish rather than just survive the AI transition. His honest admission that he has experienced both the best and worst of AI -- the sense of possibility alongside the shallow task-switching trap -- gives the framework practical grounding.
points: Setting ethical AI boundaries before edge cases arise is more important than the exact lines drawn -- the process of deciding what you will and won't use AI for forces clarity of purpose that prevents drift.

AI's time savings almost never translate into rest or leisure without an intentional 'vision' for saved time; without it, the gravitational pull is simply to do more work and the efficiency gain is lost.
Mastering one AI tool deeply produces better results than sampling many superficially -- pick one, use it consistently, and build genuine understanding of its underlying logic before expanding.
Prompting is not a new technical skill for teachers to acquire; it is an application of the task-explanation expertise teachers already possess, structured as Role + Task + Format.

AI is excellent at administrative tasks (research, drafting, differentiation, quiz creation) but assessing student work is a clear ethical boundary worth preserving -- the line between human judgment and AI delegation matters for professional integrity.
quotes: I want you to teach and lead with excellence in this rapidly-changing world. And when I imagine what that looks like, I think of you having: Deep rest, Meaningful work, Continual improvement, Equipped and engaged students, The exercising of creativity within your craft.
AI is not the answer. But it can be part of the answer. It can also make things a lot worse. And if I'm honest, at different times over the last year I've experienced the best and worst of AI.

Just because you could use AI to do something, doesn't mean you should. Jurassic Park - need I say more. AI is excellent at tasks that require raw administrative horsepower such as research, drafting, differentiation, quiz creation, resource generation.
Here's the irony of AI: It saves us heaps of time but it can leave us busier than ever... The gravity of AI is such that we will be drawn to using our saved time just to do more.

Pick one tool and learn it well. I use Claude as my daily driver... Sticking with one tool and using it well will prevent you from flitting from tool-to-tool and failing to build an understanding of the basic ideas.

Prompting may sound technical or complicated, but it's actually quite simple, and if you're a teacher, here's some good news: you're already great at prompting. Why? Because prompting is just explaining a task, and this is something you're excellent at!
I structure my prompts like this: Role: tell the AI how you want it to act. Task: tell the AI what it is doing. Format: tell the AI how you want the material.
